tools.name: query
tools.title: Query Repository
tools.description:
<WHY>
DuckDB SQL over the parsed graph — code, git history, data files, external MCP tools, one surface. Every operation returns a table, and tables compose: joins, CTEs, LATERAL, recursive traversals. A failed query is cheap — run SUMMARIZE <view> or EXPLAIN first when guessing shape. Prefer explore/read when they fit; query is for counting, listing, traversing, joining.
</WHY>

<VIEWS>
Files — uri, path, dirname, name, extension, mime, byte_size, content_category (code|document|structured-data|…), headline, summary, structure, token_count, mtime
Functions — uri, file, name, qualified_name, function_kind, declaring_type, declaring_type_qualified, visibility, signature, return_type, parameters, lang, is_static, is_async, start_line, end_line
Types — uri, file, name, qualified_name, type_kind, namespace, signature, extends, implements, lang, start_line, end_line
Annotations — lint/SARIF findings: rule_id, severity, message, document_uri, target_uri
Language-specific views exist (csharp_types, python_imports, markdown_headings, …) — explore help:/// to discover them.
</VIEWS>

<FUNCTIONS>
search_pipeline(query, scope, k) → uri, score, headline, structure — hybrid semantic+lexical
glob_files('src/**/*.cs;!**/tests/**') → uri · matches_glob(uri, pattern)
grep_matches(pattern, scope, max_results) → uri, line_number, line_content · regex_matches(…)
git_status() · git_diff() · git_blame() · git_hotspots() · git_patches()
parse(text) — CSV/JSON/YAML → table · xlsx(uri, sheet) · ask(jsonData, intent, maxTokens) — LLM synthesis over rows
</FUNCTIONS>

<EXAMPLE>
SELECT uri, round(score, 3) AS score FROM search_pipeline('config loading', k := 5);
</EXAMPLE>

Budget: results auto-summarize past your tokenBudget — set it to the most you'd pay for the answer.

tools.name: read
tools.title: Read Content
tools.description:
Read indexed files, symbols or line ranges. Budget chooses content -> structure -> clipped -> headline. Narrow for depth; widen for breadth.

URI glob = URI patterns combined with ; and excluded with !
URI pattern = [scheme + path glob][#fragment]
; combines includes; ! excludes from ALL includes. Fragment-only exclusions apply across included files.

Schemes: file:/// (this repo), github://owner/repo/ (imports), help:/// (docs), concept:/// and vocabulary:/// (repo memory).
Bare literal-leading paths use file:///; patterns starting with *, ? or [ match across schemes.

Path globs: * = zero or more characters within one / segment; ? = one character; ** = zero or more path segments, as a whole segment; [abc] [a-z] = character sets/ranges; {a,b} = alternatives, multiplying across groups. Percent-encode literal metacharacters: %2A, %5B, %7B.

Fragments:
#symbol=Name: qualified name or dotted suffix.
#symbol=*Service: symbol-name wildcard; * can span qualification dots.
#symbol=C.* / #symbol=C.**: direct members / all descendants; C must be concrete.
#kind=P, #visibility=P, #extends=P, #implements=P: declaration filters; P is a pattern. Filters alone imply #symbol=*.
#line=N or #line=N,M: 1-based inclusive lines.
& combines fragment params; line constraints intersect symbol spans.
#heading-slug: document anchor.
#/path: JSON Pointer; ~0 escapes ~, ~1 escapes /. # selects root; #/ selects an empty key. & inside a pointer is key data.

Case: paths, wildcard queries and declaration filters are insensitive; literal source fragments preserve case.

file:///src/{api,core}/**/*.cs#kind=interface&visibility=public;!**/generated/**
App.cs#symbol=App.Run;config.json#/logging;README.md#line=1,12

Depth: help:///tools/uri-patterns.md

tools.name: explain
tools.title: Explain Repository
tools.description:
<WHY>
Delegate understanding to an army of fast exploration agents. Before reading many files to understand the shape of the system, fire off multiple scoped explains in parallel to investigate your questions for you.
It reads widely, synthesizes, and reports back with citations. You get comprehension, not raw text.

Their tokens are much cheaper than yours while still being very effective for this work. Trust but verify their work with targeted followup reads. 
</WHY>

<WHEN_TO_USE>
Use explain when you want a synthesized answer about a scoped area of the repository.

Good questions:
- "How does JWT refresh work in AuthService?"
- "What authentication methods does service X support?"
- "Why does PaymentProcessor use idempotency keys?"
- "What happens when an item is indexed, step by step?"
- "What are the relevant keywords related to bearer tokens?"

Bad questions:
- "Explain everything about authentication"
- "What does this service do?" without a meaningful scope
</WHEN_TO_USE>

<OUTPUT>
Returns a synthesized answer with citations derived from the explain service's tool use.
Verify important claims against the cited code when the stakes are high.
</OUTPUT>

<PARAMETERS>
`question`: required and should be a full sentence
`keywords`: required - the symbols, files, or terms-of-art you want explain to focus on. You almost always know these better than a generic extraction would infer (you just ran explore, or you already know the symbols).
`uriGlob` optionally scopes the answer with the full power of uri globbing — a hard filter on what is searched, not a soft bias. Omit it to use the current repository.
`tokenBudget` controls how much room the synthesized answer has. Does not affect the input token budget for the agent producing the answer.
</PARAMETERS>

Full sentences work best."},"keywords":{"type":"string","description":"The symbols, files, or terms-of-art the explain service should focus on. Omit for the local repository. Incorrect names return the valid names.","default":null}},"required":["question","keywords"]}

tools.name: execute
tools.title: Execute JavaScript
tools.description:
<WHY>
When query and read together aren't enough, drop into sandboxed JavaScript with all RepoQL data, the file system, and approved MCP tools at hand. Compose what doesn't exist as a single tool; store reusable modules so the next composition is one import away.
</WHY>

<WHEN_TO_USE>
- Non-text artifacts — graphviz SVG/PNG, ffmpeg probes
- Imperative shape — branch on intermediate values, accumulate across iterations, retry
- Writing outputs back into the sandbox for later steps
- Prefer query when one SQL statement would do — the generated mcp_* macros already join external tools with graph data.
</WHEN_TO_USE>

<FUNCTIONS>
repoql.query(sql) → rows · repoql.read(uriGlob, {budget}) → {content, representation, tokensUsed}
repoql.write(uri, content) — sandbox write scope, repo-rooted · repoql.delete(uri) — default .repoql/tmp/**
repoql.graphviz(dot) → SVG · repoql.svgToPng(svg) · repoql.ffmpeg({input, output, args, probe})
mcp.servers() · mcp.tools("github") · mcp.describe("github", "search_issues") · mcp.github.search_issues({...}) — approved MCP tools, parsed results
import("yaml"), import("diff"), import("semver"), and other built-in modules
</FUNCTIONS>

Return plain JavaScript values — objects and arrays render as tables; console output is captured.

tools.name: explore
tools.title: Explore Repository
tools.description:
<WHY>
The index already knows everything. Explore searches it exhaustively — hybrid lexical + semantic — and shows what exists, ranked by how well it answers you. One call reveals the landscape AND the vocabulary: the real class names and terms-of-art for everything after. Without it you're guessing names and grepping blind.
</WHY>

<WORKFLOW>
1. Explore broadly — keywords="authentication", question="where is authentication handled?" → discovers JwtTokenValidator, SessionMiddleware
2. Explore with intent — refined keywords plus a specific question; rerank promotes what ANSWERS over what merely mentions
3. Read precisely — read("file:///src/Auth.cs#symbol=JwtTokenValidator.Validate", 800)
4. Iterate with the vocabulary you just learned

Vocabulary cold — new codebase, terms borrowed from elsewhere? Run discover_vocabulary first, then explore WITH what it returns. Same when matches come back weak: weak hits usually mean your words, not the repo. The first explore is never wasted — even unexpected results teach you what IS there.
</WORKFLOW>

<PARAMETERS>
keywords — the probe: class names, concepts, short phrases; no filler.
question — your intent; results are ordered by how well they answer it, not just match. Omit only when surveying.
uriGlob — scope, full glob grammar (see server instructions). Unscoped spans every imported repo plus help:///, noisier than you usually want. "file:///**" is the right default; "help:///**" searches the docs like code.
breadth — spreads detail across useful matches: 2 favors the strongest, 10 spreads more evenly, 0 auto from match strengths. Very weak matches do not become useful just because breadth increases.
tokenBudget — maximum result tokens, not a target to fill. Useful matches get addresses and relevance scores first; spare room adds structure and available snippets. Read the exact symbol when you need its body. Omit the budget and the server picks; the footer shows a cap only when you named one.
</PARAMETERS>

Depth: help:///tools/explore.md

tools.title: Discover Vocabulary
tools.description:
Discover the repository's names for what you mean. Give the words you have; get names grounded in code, concepts, and captured vocabulary, with evidence for the next search.

<WHEN_TO_USE>
- You know what you need, but not what this repository calls it.
- Before explore on an unfamiliar repository or subsystem, including imports. Unfamiliar ground is the cue: plausible search results can conceal the local names you lack.
</WHEN_TO_USE>

tools.name: capture_concept
tools.title: Capture Concept
tools.description:
<WHY>
Concepts are source controlled — the repository's permanent memory. Record durable ideas about this repo, not transient user context. They are fact-checked against their evidence and kept honest over time: a great investment in your future.
</WHY>

<WHEN_TO_USE>
- You learned a durable idea about this repository that future agents should inherit
- A hard-won lesson would prevent the same mistake later

Not this: user identity, preferences, session-scoped asks — per-agent memory holds those. Nor a bug tracker: a defect you can fix belongs in a fix, not a capsule.
</WHEN_TO_USE>

<CAPSULES>
One form, five categories:
- principle — what we are doing here: the outcomes we want and what we refuse on the way. Always universal, no relevance, no verification.
- wisdom — a timeless idea about how to think.
- rule — an invariant or guardrail: what must not break.
- shape — what keeps the repository coherent as it grows: where things belong and the form they take. Relevance is the location.
- knowledge — a file map or architecture fact; verification required so it stays true.
</CAPSULES>

<MECHANICS>
relevance — semicolon-delimited URI globs; the concept surfaces when an agent touches a matching file. Cover where the idea applies, not where it was learned.
isUniversal — required, and written to the capsule either way. true also loads it into the always-on index every agent carries: earn that only if the concept can be violated outside its relevance globs.
verification — URI globs or web URLs that fact-check the claim, at capture and on a schedule. Anchor at the proof: #symbol=NAME re-resolves as code moves, #line=M,N pins a range. Required for knowledge, optional for rule and shape, refused for principle and wisdom. With it give ttlDays, the days the evidence stays trusted.
Files land in .repoql/concepts/<category>/<subcategory?>/<Name>.md, readable at the matching concept:/// URI
</MECHANICS>

Worked examples: help:///tools/capture-concept.md

tools.name: capture_vocabulary
tools.title: Capture Vocabulary
tools.description:
<WHY>
A repository-specific term learned once should not be rediscovered. Capture leaves the real term behind with the outside-world words that made it hard to find, so later sessions can reach it through discover_vocabulary.
</WHY>

<WHEN_TO_USE>
Use this at the moment you learn a repository-specific name through investigation, especially when the wording you began with does not appear in code. Meanings stay to one judgeable sentence; mechanisms, rules, and warnings belong in capture_concept instead.
</WHEN_TO_USE>

<BEHAVIOR>
The host normalizes the row into .repoql/vocabulary.csv and returns its vocabulary:/// address. Each alias is checked through the indexed text surface; an alias already present in the corpus is flagged as redundant but still captured. Repeating the same term plus domain replaces that sense.
</BEHAVIOR>

tools.name: command
tools.title: Run Command
tools.description:
<WHY>
Your remote control for the host — start, stop, configure, diagnose, and manage imports. Commands follow the same shape as the CLI: command words, then explicit `--option value` arguments, so anything you can do at the terminal you can do here.
</WHY>

<SYNTAX>
`command(command="<command> <subcommand> --param value")`

- `command(command="help")` lists every available command; `<cmd> --help` gives usage for one.
- Most reached for: `host status` · `host restart` · `diagnostics memory` · `config list` · `account whoami` · `dashboard`
- Arguments are explicit options: `config set --key search.rerank_enabled --value true`.
</SYNTAX>

Examples: \u0022help\u0022, \u0022config list\u0022, \u0022config read --key search.rerank_enabled\u0022, \u0022config set --key search.rerank_enabled --value true\u0022, \u0022account whoami\u0022, \u0022import list\u0022, \u0022host status\u0022, \u0022host reindex --glob file:///src/**\u0022."} },"required":["command"]}

tools.name: import
tools.title: Import External Source
tools.description:
<WHY>
Import pulls more of the world into the graph — other repos, S3 buckets, sarif reports, test coverage — and every other tool reaches them with the same URIs. Import multiplies the usefulness of everything else.
</WHY>

<SOURCES>
- GitHub: github://owner/repo, or @ref to pin
- Git: git://host/path · https://host/path.git@ref · ssh://git@host/path · git@host:path.git
- S3 bucket: s3://bucket/prefix/ — read-only, indexed in place; large or binary objects kept as searchable metadata
- Local directory: local:///absolute/path, ".", or a plain path — live-watched, never cloned or mutated
- SARIF report: sarif:///absolute/path.sarif (roslyn/snyk/sonarqube/…)
- code coverage coverage: coverage://absolute/path.coburtura (most formats supported)
</SOURCES>

<WHEN_TO_USE>
- The task benefits from detail you don't have locally
- Comparing or tracing flows and history across repositories
- Valuable annotations exist that you want joined against the graph
</WHEN_TO_USE>

<GUIDANCE>
import("github://owner/repo") · import("github://owner/repo@v1.2.0") · import(".")
Remove with a leading "-": import("-github://owner/repo") — deletes the import and its indexed data; local files are never touched.
A local git checkout is promoted to its canonical github:///git:// identity. Re-importing updates incrementally; annotation re-import replaces.
An import's captured memory comes with it: concepts at concept:///<scheme>/<owner>/<repo>/**, vocabulary at vocabulary:///<scheme>/<owner>/<repo>/**, scoping rebased to the import's address.
Git/VFS imports return immediately with an operation id and the SQL to track progress; annotations complete synchronously. 
All current imports: SELECT * FROM Filesystems.
</GUIDANCE>

Depth: help:///tools/import.md

S3 is imported read-only. Local git checkouts are imported in place, live-watched, promoted to their canonical github:// or git:// identity when possible, and never mutated. tools.name: watch
tools.title: Watch Process Telemetry
tools.description:
<WHY>
You can't improve what you can't measure. Watch launches a process with RepoQL as its OTEL collector — traces, logs, and metrics land in queryable tables while it runs, plus sampled CPU/memory for the whole process tree. Evidence you can query repeatedly instead of output you read once.
</WHY>

<WHEN_TO_USE>
- Observe an app without spending tokens reading all its output
- Profile as part of optimization
- Diagnose exceptions, crashes, hangs, or slow startup
</WHEN_TO_USE>

<ENVIRONMENT>
environment passes extra vars as key=value;key2=value2. The process inherits the host environment, then your overrides; RepoQL's OTLP exporter vars always win, so capture cannot be broken. %VAR% references expand; escape a literal ; or = with \. Use it to switch on an app's own telemetry — e.g. CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1;OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 for Claude Code.
</ENVIRONMENT>

<LIFECYCLE>
Returns immediately with run_id, telemetry_schema, and starter queries — the process keeps running while you query its telemetry. The run ends when the process exits (<schema>.watch_run.completed_at flips from NULL). There is no MCP-callable stop: kill the process at its source; restarting the host disposes every active run.
</LIFECYCLE>

Full reference: help:///tools/watch/watch.md · Watching Claude Code: help:///tools/watch/watching-claude.md
